newsitem.title: USA: CBOE develops screen-based trading system.
newsitem.headline: CBOE develops screen-based trading system.

text.p: The Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE) has been developing a screen-based trading system without any decision yet on what to list or whether to use it as an after-hours trading facility or for other purposes, CBOE leaders said.

"We don't know what (contracts) we'll put on it, we don't know where we'll put it, we don't know when we'll use it," Thomas Ascher, CBOE vice chairman, said in an interview with Reuters while attending a risk management conference here.
"We're working on the front-end (terminals for users) of the system," added CBOE chairman Alger "Duke" Chapman.
"We will then, in conjunction with the Options Clearing Corp, sell a total package to people who wish to aquire screen-based trading and clearing and risk-management systems," Chapman said.

After signing a letter of intent to develop a screen-based system with the Swiss Options and Futures Exchange (SOFEX) and Options Clearing Corp last year, CBOE has maintained a low key on the project.
"We have taken that letter of intent and turned it into a contract," Chapman said. "So right now, a formal contract and work have started."
But another senior exchange official contacted earlier in the week declined to comment about the trading system, saying the project was still in its early stages.
Though CBOE has been the forerunner in embracing technological change, electronic trading has been a controversial issue at some of Chicago's exchanges, which were built on the open outcry system.

Last year, when the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) decided in a member vote to make agricultural contract trading on its afterhours, electronic Project A system permanent after a pilot program, CBOT chairman Patrick Arbor called it an "emotional issue."
Ascher, who is also a designated primary market-maker for one of the most heavily traded issues on the CBOE floor, said he would not be entirely happy if his options were traded electronically.

"I think it (a decision on screen-based system) will be a function of perceived opportunity," Ascher said. He said the system could be used for trading outside CBOE's normal business hours and/or for trading in contracts that "do not have the critical mass to trade in open-outcry."
Technological development for the new system was hoped to be completed by the end of 1997, but the exchange has yet to set a timetable for the rest of the project, the officials said.
